title: Increased cyclicity of atomic transitions via coherent interference of decay paths
summary: Optical readout is a fundamental tool in atomic state measurement, yet the fidelity of optical readout is frequently limited by imperfect photon collection. This can be mitigated when readout occurs on a cycling transition which continuously fluoresces under resonant excitation, thus increasing signal and enabling single-shot readout. We present a method to extend the cyclicity of atomic transitions via coherent destructive interference between spurious decay paths. We describe the characteristics of atomic systems in which this method can be implemented and model several examples in which the number of emitted photons is increased by multiple orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method to extend the cyclicity of atomic transitions using coherent destructive interference between spurious decay paths, improving optical readout fidelity by increasing photon emission by orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Optical readout fidelity is limited by imperfect photon collection. Cycling transitions that continuously fluoresce can mitigate this, but many atomic systems lack naturally cycling transitions due to spurious decay paths.
AI.method: The authors propose using coherent destructive interference between spurious decay paths to suppress unwanted decays, thereby extending the cyclicity of atomic transitions. They characterize the conditions under which atomic systems can implement this approach.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on several model atomic systems, where the number of emitted photons is increased by multiple orders of magnitude compared to non-cyclic transitions.
AI.conclusion: Coherent destructive interference of spurious decay paths is a viable strategy to create effectively cycling transitions in atomic systems, significantly improving single-shot optical readout capabilities.

title: Existence of Large Boundary Layer Solutions for the Outflow Problem of Full Compressible Navier-Stokes Equations
summary: We investigate the existence and non-existence of large-amplitude boundary layer solutions to the outflow problem for the one-dimensional full compressible Navier-Stokes equations on the half-line $\mathbb{R}_+$. Through a delicate global phase-plane analysis, we substantially extend the small-amplitude boundary layer solutions obtained via the center-manifold approach to the large-amplitude regime. Based on the sign of $M_+-1$ (with $M_+$ denoting the Mach number at the right end state) and the Prandtl-number-related parameter $ζ$, we provide a complete characterization of the existence and non-existence of large-amplitude boundary layer solutions for this half-space outflow problem. In sharp contrast to the corresponding inflow problem, boundary layer solutions to the outflow problem are permitted to be non-monotone, and their existence region in the phase plane can be an open set.

AI.tldr: This paper studies large-amplitude boundary layer solutions for the outflow problem of one-dimensional full compressible Navier-Stokes equations on a half-line. Using global phase-plane analysis, the authors extend prior small-amplitude results (obtained via center-manifold methods) to the large-amplitude regime, providing a complete characterization of existence/non-existence based on the Mach number sign and a Prandtl-number-related parameter.
AI.motivation: Previous work only established small-amplitude boundary layer solutions via center-manifold approaches for the outflow problem. A complete mathematical understanding of large-amplitude solutions is needed, and the structure of these solutions was previously unknown.
AI.method: The authors employ a delicate global phase-plane analysis to investigate boundary layer solutions, examining the existence and non-existence based on the sign of M_+-1 (Mach number at the right end state) and the Prandtl-number-related parameter ζ.
AI.result: The paper provides a complete characterization of large-amplitude boundary layer solutions. In contrast to the inflow problem, these solutions can be non-monotone, and their existence region in the phase plane can be an open set.
AI.conclusion: The large-amplitude boundary layer solutions for the outflow problem exhibit fundamentally different and richer structure compared to the inflow problem, including the possibility of non-monotone profiles and open existence regions in phase space.

title: Early-Time Reshaping of Laser-Induced Plasma Profiles
summary: Laser-induced plasmas are primarily characterized by their temporal density decay. Using time-resolved transverse optical diffractometry, we reveal their concurrent spatial evolution, demonstrating pronounced broadening and flattening during the first 200 ps following ionization. This non-self-similar evolution arises from the local density dependence of electron-ion recombination, without particle transport. Exploiting the continuum of initial densities within a single plasma disc, we experimentally reconstruct an effective, time-dependent local recombination law over a broad density range. Applied locally to independently measured initial plasma profiles, this kinetic map quantitatively predicts their subsequent evolution. These results are relevant to transient diffractive optics, plasma-based optical elements and waveguides, and the development of laser-induced plasmas as platforms for gas-phase THz plasmonics.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals the spatial evolution of laser-induced plasmas using time-resolved transverse optical diffractometry, showing that they broaden and flatten within the first 200 ps due to density-dependent electron-ion recombination rather than particle transport. The authors reconstruct a local recombination law from a single plasma disc and use it to predict subsequent plasma evolution.
AI.motivation: Laser-induced plasmas have been primarily characterized by temporal density decay, while their concurrent spatial evolution has remained unexplored. Understanding this spatial dynamics is important for applications in diffractive optics, plasma-based optical elements, and THz plasmonics.
AI.method: The authors use time-resolved transverse optical diffractometry to measure both temporal and spatial plasma evolution. They exploit the continuum of initial densities within a single plasma disc to experimentally reconstruct an effective, time-dependent local recombination law over a broad density range. This kinetic map is then applied locally to independently measured initial plasma profiles to predict their evolution.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates pronounced broadening and flattening of the plasma spatial profile during the first 200 ps following ionization. This non-self-similar evolution is attributed to the local density dependence of electron-ion recombination, not particle transport. The reconstructed recombination law quantitatively predicts subsequent plasma evolution.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish that laser-induced plasma spatial dynamics are governed by local density-dependent recombination, providing a predictive framework relevant to transient diffractive optics, plasma-based optical elements, waveguides, and gas-phase THz plasmonics.

title: An hp-version time stepping spectral Monte Carlo method for semi-linear parabolic equations
summary: In this paper, we present an $hp$-version time-stepping spectral Monte Carlo method for solving semi-linear parabolic equations. The key innovation lies in constructing an exponentially accurate stochastic algorithm that integrates a residual iteration scheme on Gauss-type nodes in both temporal and spatial directions with a reconstruction strategy rooted in spectral methods. To address the long-time simulations and initial singularities that are often challenging for traditional stochastic algorithms (e.g., walk-on-spheres method), we further develop an $hp$-version time-stepping framework that employs multiple time steps and, respectively, geometric time partitions with linearly increasing polynomial degrees to handle these difficulties. Notably, the proposed algorithm bypasses the need to solve linear systems required by traditional spectral methods and remarkably supports parallel computation at both temporal and spatial grid points. We rigorously establish exponential convergence rates for the multistep method within a finite number of iterations. Extensive numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the spectral accuracy and computational efficiency of the proposed method in long-time simulations, problems with initial singularities, and a five-dimensional problem, thereby validating the theoretical results.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an hp-version time-stepping spectral Monte Carlo method for semi-linear parabolic equations, achieving exponential accuracy through a residual iteration scheme on Gauss-type nodes combined with spectral reconstruction. The method handles long-time simulations and initial singularities via geometric time partitions with increasing polynomial degrees, supports parallel computation, and avoids solving linear systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional stochastic algorithms (e.g., walk-on-spheres method) struggle with long-time simulations and initial singularities. Spectral methods require solving expensive linear systems. The authors aim to develop a stochastic algorithm that achieves high accuracy while overcoming these limitations.
AI.method: The method combines: (1) a residual iteration scheme on Gauss-type nodes in both temporal and spatial directions, (2) spectral-based reconstruction strategies, (3) an hp-version time-stepping framework using multiple time steps with geometric time partitions and linearly increasing polynomial degrees, and (4) a Monte Carlo approach that bypasses linear system solves and supports parallel computation.
AI.result: The authors rigorously establish exponential convergence rates for the multistep method within a finite number of iterations. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate spectral accuracy and computational efficiency for long-time simulations, problems with initial singularities, and a five-dimensional problem.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hp-version time-stepping spectral Monte Carlo method provides a computationally efficient, parallel-friendly, and exponentially convergent approach for solving semi-linear parabolic equations, addressing key limitations of traditional stochastic and spectral methods.

title: Attractor-Basin-Limited Fidelity in Reproducible Multistate Vortex Memory
summary: Multilevel non-volatile memory technologies face recurring trade-offs among information density, endurance, retention, and switching energy. We investigate an alternative state variable based on the discrete vortex configuration of self-organized vortices in a boundary-driven electron fluid. A dissipative point-vortex model derived from magnetohydrodynamic dynamics yields six reproducible vortex codewords, corresponding to 2.585 bits per cell, whose write fidelity, noise sensitivity, 100-cycle endurance, and effective information capacity are quantified. The ordering of their finite-amplitude basin radii $r_{50}$ differs from that predicted by both fixed-circulation and fully coupled linear-stability spectra. A nonlinear saddle-point construction based on the reduced dynamics likewise does not recover the measured basin ordering. The discrepancy is associated with escape pathways involving coupled position--circulation dynamics that are absent from the fixed-circulation description. These results show that local stability alone does not determine the finite perturbation tolerance of the vortex states considered here. The proposed memory requires active hold power, and passive retention remains to be established experimentally.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates discrete vortex configurations in a boundary-driven electron fluid as an alternative state variable for multilevel non-volatile memory. A dissipative point-vortex model produces six reproducible codewords (2.585 bits/cell), but the measured ordering of finite-amplitude basin radii differs from predictions based on both linear-stability spectra and reduced nonlinear saddle-point constructions, suggesting that coupled position-circulation escape dynamics—absent from fixed-circulation models—determine finite perturbation tolerance. The memory requires active hold power, and passive retention remains unverified.
AI.motivation: Current multilevel non-volatile memory technologies face trade-offs among density, endurance, retention, and switching energy. The authors seek an alternative state variable—discrete vortex configurations in a boundary-driven electron fluid—that may circumvent these recurring compromises.
AI.method: The authors derive a dissipative point-vortex model from magnetohydrodynamic dynamics, generate six reproducible vortex codewords, and quantify write fidelity, noise sensitivity, 100-cycle endurance, and effective information capacity. They compare basin radii ordering against predictions from fixed-circulation linear-stability spectra and a fully coupled nonlinear saddle-point construction.
AI.result: The six vortex codewords yield 2.585 bits per cell. The observed ordering of finite-amplitude basin radii r50 differs from predictions by both fixed-circulation and fully coupled linear-stability spectra, and also from the reduced nonlinear saddle-point construction, due to escape pathways involving coupled position–circulation dynamics absent from fixed-circulation descriptions. Local stability alone does not determine finite perturbation tolerance.
AI.conclusion: Vortex-configuration-based memory is feasible in principle but requires active hold power; passive retention remains to be experimentally established. Local linear stability is insufficient to predict finite perturbation robustness, motivating new theoretical approaches that account for coupled position–circulation escape dynamics.

title: A Weighted Bossel-Daners Transfer Principle and a Pure-Power Robin Faber-Krahn Inequality
summary:
We prove a weighted Bossel-Daners transfer principle for the first Robin eigenvalue of the $p$-Laplacian under $w=m^{1/p'}$, where $p'=p/(p-1)$. The argument combines double-density isoperimetry with spectral admissibility for singular weights and normalized-flux monotonicity. It uses an exact $BV$ zero-extension formula, an $L^{p'}(m\,dx)$ selection lemma, and a nonatomic rank map that remains well defined on positive-measure level sets.
  For the singular pair \[ m_b(x)=|x|^b, \qquad w_b(x)=|x|^{b/p'}, \] known power-weight isoperimetry provides the geometric input. We establish spectral admissibility up to the critical exponent $p=N$ and, for the positive radial first eigenfunction $z=z(r)$ on the centered ball $B_R$, derive the integrated singular radial equation and center asymptotics and prove directly that \[ θ_R'(r)>0 \quad(0<r<R), \qquad θ_R(r)=\frac{|z'(r)|^{p-1}}{r^{b/p'}z(r)^{p-1}}, \] with $θ_R(0)=0$ and $θ_R(R)=β$. Let $Ω\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a finite union of bounded connected Lipschitz domains whose closures are pairwise disjoint, let $Ω_b^\sharp$ be the centered ball of equal $|x|^b$-weighted volume, and let $λ_{1,β}^b$ denote the first eigenvalue for the displayed pair. Consequently, \[ λ_{1,β}^{b}(Ω_b^\sharp) \le λ_{1,β}^{b}(Ω) \] whenever $N\ge 2$, $1<p\le N$, $-p<b<0$, and $β>0$. The range $1<p<N$ is complementary to the previously known $p\ge N$ weighted Talenti theory; at the shared endpoint $p=N$, the present proof also permits the singular contact $0\in\partialΩ$.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a weighted Bossel-Daners transfer principle for the first Robin eigenvalue of the p-Laplacian with singular weights w=m^{1/p'}, combining double-density isoperimetry, spectral admissibility, and normalized-flux monotonicity, and establishes eigenvalue comparison between finite unions of Lipschitz domains and centered balls for the critical range 1<p≤N.
AI.motivation: To extend the weighted Talenti theory for Robin eigenvalues of the p-Laplacian to the complementary critical range 1<p≤N (previously known only for p≥N), handling singular weights and establishing the Bossel-Daners isoperimetric-type inequality for weighted settings.
AI.method: Combines double-density isoperimetry with spectral admissibility for singular weights and normalized-flux monotonicity. Uses an exact BV zero-extension formula, an L^{p'}(m dx) selection lemma, and a nonatomic rank map on positive-measure level sets. For the singular power pair m_b=|x|^b, w_b=|x|^{b/p'}, power-weight isoperimetry supplies geometric input, with direct verification of θ_R'(r)>0 via the integrated singular radial equation.
AI.result: Establishes spectral admissibility up to critical exponent p=N and proves λ_{1,β}^{b}(Ω_b^♯) ≤ λ_{1,β}^{b}(Ω) for N≥2, 1<p≤N, −p<b<0, β>0, covering the range 1<p<N complementary to prior p≥N theory, with the shared endpoint p=N also permitting singular contact 0∈∂Ω.
AI.conclusion: The weighted Bossel-Daners principle holds for the first Robin eigenvalue of the p-Laplacian with singular power weights in the full critical range 1<p≤N, completing the weighted Talenti-type picture across all p and including geometrically singular boundary cases at the endpoint.

title: On the feasibility of model-based feedback control of vertical instability growth rate using out-vessel coils in ARC-like scenarios
summary: In this work, we propose a model-based feedback controller that regulates the vertical instability growth rate ($γ_{gr}$) of a high-elongation, double-null tokamak directly, using only out-vessel poloidal field (PF) coils. High elongation raises the achievable plasma current and fusion performance but makes the plasma vertically unstable, and in a fusion power plant the in-vessel coils that present devices rely on for stabilization may be absent, leaving only distant out-vessel circuits. The controller couples a machine learning surrogate of non-rigid, profile agnostic vertical instability metric to a constrained quadratic program: the surrogate supplies real-time $γ_{gr}$ estimates and, via automatic differentiation, the actuator sensitivities, while the program allocates coil voltages to track a target growth rate, maintain double-null divertor balance, and respect electromechanical limits. We tested this method on the ARC~V3A power plant design configuration across 24 closed-loop simulations spanning equilibrium variations, actuator degradations, and transient disturbances. We achieved full or marginal success in 83\% of these cases (full in 50\%, marginal in a further 33\%) and lose control in the remaining 17\%; the failures map the boundary of out-vessel controllability (occurring at the highest growth rates) and under actuator limits. The controller does not regulate boundary shape explicitly: separatrix geometry follows indirectly from growth rate and flux balance control and would require a separate shape control layer for sustained scenario evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a model-based feedback controller for regulating vertical instability growth rate (γ_gr) in high-elongation, double-null tokamaks using only out-vessel poloidal field coils. The controller combines a machine learning surrogate with a constrained quadratic program, tested across 24 closed-loop simulations on the ARC V3A power plant design, achieving 83% success (full or marginal) with failures mapping controllability boundaries.
AI.motivation: High elongation improves plasma current and fusion performance but creates vertical instability. Fusion power plants may lack in-vessel stabilization coils, leaving only distant out-vessel circuits. This creates a need for a control strategy that can stabilize vertical instabilities using only out-vessel coils, which is challenging due to the distance and reduced coupling.
AI.method: The controller couples (1) a machine learning surrogate of a non-rigid, profile-agnostic vertical instability metric that provides real-time γ_gr estimates and actuator sensitivities via automatic differentiation, with (2) a constrained quadratic program that allocates coil voltages to track a target growth rate, maintain double-null divertor balance, and respect electromechanical limits.
AI.result: Tested on the ARC V3A power plant configuration across 24 closed-loop simulations spanning equilibrium variations, actuator degradations, and transient disturbances. Achieved full or marginal success in 83% of cases (50% full, 33% marginal), losing control in 17%. Failures occurred at the highest growth rates and under actuator limits, mapping the boundary of out-vessel controllability.
AI.conclusion: Out-vessel coil-based control of vertical instability growth rate is feasible within certain controllability boundaries, but the controller does not regulate boundary shape explicitly—separatrix geometry follows indirectly from growth rate and flux balance control, requiring a separate shape control layer for sustained scenario evolution.

title: Accurately computing quasiperiodic parabolic equations within finite-size domains via modeling quasiperiodic boundary conditions
summary: Quasiperiodic systems exhibit long-range order without decay and are naturally posed on the whole space. However, in practical applications, computations are performed on finite domains, making the choice of boundary conditions that preserve the global quasiperiodic structure a key modeling challenge. In particular, conventional boundary conditions contain no information about the quasiperiodic field beyond the computational domain. Traditional periodic boundary conditions (PBCs) suffer from Diophantine errors due to the rational approximation of irrational numbers, limiting their accuracy. Motivated by this, we propose a class of quasiperiodic boundary conditions (QBCs) for quasiperiodic problems, which avoid the limitations caused by traditional Diophantine errors. By exploiting a homomorphism between a low-dimensional physical domain and a high-dimensional torus, QBCs effectively capture the long-range structure at the boundaries. To validate the proposed approach, we apply QBCs to solve quasiperiodic parabolic equations (QPEs) within finite-size domains and establish rigorous convergence results. Numerical experiments demonstrate that QBCs substantially reduce the influence of Diophantine errors. When employed to model finite-size QPEs and combined with suitable numerical discretizations, they enable accurate and efficient computations for both high- and low-regularity cases, while exhibiting improved convergence compared with PBCs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes quasiperiodic boundary conditions (QBCs) for solving quasiperiodic problems on finite domains, avoiding the Diophantine errors inherent in traditional periodic boundary conditions (PBCs). By exploiting a homomorphism between the low-dimensional physical domain and high-dimensional torus, QBCs capture long-range quasiperiodic structure at boundaries and demonstrate superior convergence for quasiperiodic parabolic equations.
AI.motivation: Quasiperiodic systems are naturally defined on the whole space, but computations require finite domains. Conventional boundary conditions (especially periodic ones) suffer from Diophantine errors due to rational approximation of irrational frequencies, limiting accuracy. There is a need for boundary conditions that preserve the global quasiperiodic structure within finite computational domains.
AI.method: The authors propose a class of quasiperiodic boundary conditions (QBCs) that leverage a homomorphism between the low-dimensional physical domain and a higher-dimensional torus, enabling boundaries to capture the long-range quasiperiodic structure. They apply QBCs to solve quasiperiodic parabolic equations (QPEs) on finite domains and establish rigorous convergence results, combining them with suitable numerical discretizations.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that QBCs substantially reduce the influence of Diophantine errors compared to PBCs. When applied to finite-size QPEs with suitable numerical discretizations, QBCs enable accurate and efficient computations for both high- and low-regularity cases, with improved convergence over PBCs.
AI.conclusion: QBCs provide a superior alternative to PBCs for quasiperiodic problems on finite domains, overcoming the limitations of Diophantine errors and effectively capturing long-range quasiperiodic structure at boundaries, leading to better accuracy and convergence.

title: Precise Modeling of a Complex Solenoidal Magnetic Field Using a Combination of Analytic Functions and a PINN
comment: 54 pages, 18 figures, 6 tables; includes 19 pages of supplementary material. Submitted to APL Machine Learning
summary: We demonstrate an iterative approach to modeling a sparsely measured magnetic field in a large-bore solenoid. This approach uses a hybrid of traditional and machine learning techniques. The traditional technique is a linear least-squares fit using a series solution to Laplace's equation, while the machine learning technique involves the training of a physics-informed neural network (PINN) on the least-squares fit residuals. We use a newly defined activation function "DELTAsnake," a modification to the snake activation function proposed by Ziyin et al. that allows for stronger curvature and non-monotonicity. The combined model approximately obeys Maxwell's equations to a level sufficient for producing high quality physics simulations and analysis. Our approach is applied to a highly realistic calculation of the expected magnetic field in the Mu2e experiment's Detector Solenoid which includes a simple model for the expected statistical measurement uncertainties. Using ten toy measurement simulations, we demonstrate the capabilities of our model in comparison to the least-squares method alone; the least-squares method alone results in a reduced chi-squared statistic of ${2.15 \pm 0.01}$, while our approach improves the reduced chi-square to ${1.034 \pm 0.005}$. Furthermore, for an average toy simulation, we show that the range of the RMS of the three field component residuals reduces from ${0.07-0.37}$ Gauss to ${0.05-0.07}$ Gauss. We find that this novel method is robust against a realistic systematic uncertainty deriving from Hall probe calibration bias and can be used to significantly reduce the number of measurements required to achieve an accurate model.

AI.tldr: An iterative hybrid approach combining least-squares fitting with a physics-informed neural network (using a new "DELTAsnake" activation function) to model sparsely measured magnetic fields in a large-bore solenoid, significantly improving accuracy over least-squares alone in the Mu2e experiment's Detector Solenoid.
AI.motivation: Traditional least-squares fitting to series solutions of Laplace's equation alone is insufficiently accurate for modeling sparsely measured magnetic fields in large-bore solenoids, particularly for high-quality physics simulations requiring precise field knowledge.
AI.method: A hybrid approach combining (1) a linear least-squares fit using a series solution to Laplace's equation, followed by (2) training a physics-informed neural network (PINN) on the residuals, using a newly defined "DELTAsnake" activation function (a modification of the snake activation allowing stronger curvature and non-monotonicity) to ensure the combined model approximately satisfies Maxwell's equations.
AI.result: Applied to the Mu2e Detector Solenoid with ten toy simulations: the approach improves reduced chi-squared from 2.15±0.01 (least-squares alone) to 1.034±0.005, reduces the RMS range of three field component residuals from 0.07-0.37 Gauss to 0.05-0.07 Gauss, is robust against Hall probe calibration bias, and can reduce the number of required measurements.
AI.conclusion: The novel hybrid method significantly outperforms traditional least-squares fitting alone, is robust to systematic uncertainties, and offers the potential to reduce measurement requirements while maintaining accurate magnetic field models for physics experiments.

title: A partial answer to Brezis' Open Problem 2.1
comment: 12 pages. Comments and suggestions are most welcome
summary: In this paper, we give a partial answer to Brezis' Open Problem~2.1, which concerns the uniqueness of solutions to the Ginzburg--Landau equation in the unit disc with the degree-one boundary condition. Let $λ_1$ be the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-Δ$ in the unit disc and set $\varepsilon_*:=λ_1^{-1/2}$. We prove that there exists $δ>0$ such that the radial solution is the unique weak solution for every $\varepsilon\in(\varepsilon_*-δ,\infty)$. More generally, we establish the analogous uniqueness result for the Ginzburg--Landau system on bounded connected $C^{1,1}$ domains in $\mathbb R^N$, $2\leq N\leq4$, with nontrivial boundary data. In particular, uniqueness persists slightly below the convexity threshold $\varepsilon_*$, where the strict convexity argument is no longer available. The proof combines strict convexity for $\varepsilon\geq\varepsilon_*$ with a compactness argument, nondegeneracy of the solution at $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_*$ and the implicit function theorem.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a partial answer to Brezis' Open Problem 2.1 by proving that the radial solution is the unique weak solution to the Ginzburg-Landau equation in the unit disc for all epsilon in an interval extending slightly below the critical threshold epsilon_* (the inverse square root of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue). This result is generalized to bounded connected C^1,1 domains in R^N (2≤N≤4) with nontrivial boundary data.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses Brezis' Open Problem 2.1 concerning the uniqueness of solutions to the Ginzburg-Landau equation with degree-one boundary conditions in the unit disc, extending uniqueness results below the convexity threshold epsilon_* where standard strict convexity arguments fail.
AI.method: The proof combines several techniques: (1) strict convexity arguments for the regime epsilon ≥ epsilon_*, (2) a compactness argument to handle the regime slightly below epsilon_*, (3) nondegeneracy of the solution at the critical value epsilon = epsilon_*, and (4) the implicit function theorem to extend uniqueness locally.
AI.result: The authors prove there exists δ>0 such that the radial solution is the unique weak solution for every ε ∈ (ε_*−δ, ∞). They also establish analogous uniqueness results for the Ginzburg-Landau system on bounded connected C^1,1 domains in R^N for 2≤N≤4 with nontrivial boundary data, showing uniqueness persists slightly below the convexity threshold.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully extends the uniqueness result for Ginzburg-Landau solutions below the convexity threshold epsilon_*, providing a partial answer to Brezis' Open Problem 2.1 and demonstrating that uniqueness persists in a neighborhood below the critical threshold where convexity arguments are no longer available.

title: Areal-time disruption prediction and mitigation system for the EXL-50U spherical torus
summary: This work presents a real-time disruption prediction and mitigation system developed for high-current operations in the EXL-50U Spherical Torus. By leveraging Reflective Memory (RFM) technology, the system establishes a low-latency real-time data path, creating a fully integrated pipeline that synchronizes multi-channel diagnostic acquisition, online preprocessing, real-time inference, and Massive Gas Injection (MGI) triggering. At its core, a lightweight prediction model based on a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with a channel attention mechanism extracts disruption precursor features while adaptively weighting the importance of different diagnostic channels. {Tested across discharges \#14036--\#14790, the system achieves a true positive rate of 82.4\% and a false positive rate of 16.5\%, with end-to-end latency below $1~\mathrm{ms}$ in online operation.} Mitigation experiments further show that the MGI system can supply the required gas inventory and trigger a rapid post-injection plasma response, supporting the operational requirements of EXL-50U and providing engineering guidance for future devices such as EHL-2. These results confirm the engineering feasibility of integrated real-time disruption control on EXL-50U, offering a robust basis for future research in higher-parameter fusion devices.

AI.tldr: A real-time disruption prediction and mitigation system for the EXL-50U Spherical Torus using Reflective Memory technology, a TCN-based lightweight model with channel attention, and MGI triggering. It achieves 82.4% true positive rate, 16.5% false positive rate, and sub-1ms latency across discharges #14036–#14790.
AI.motivation: High-current fusion devices require real-time disruption prediction and mitigation to protect plasma-facing components and ensure safe operation, but this demands an integrated low-latency pipeline that is challenging to build.
AI.method: The system uses Reflective Memory (RFM) for low-latency data transfer, creating a fully integrated pipeline covering multi-channel diagnostics, online preprocessing, real-time inference with a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) augmented by channel attention, and Massive Gas Injection (MGI) triggering.
AI.result: Across discharges #14036–#14790, the system achieves a true positive rate of 82.4%, false positive rate of 16.5%, and end-to-end latency below 1 ms. MGI experiments confirm adequate gas supply and rapid post-injection plasma response.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates engineering feasibility of integrated real-time disruption control on EXL-50U, providing guidance for future higher-parameter devices like EHL-2.

title: On Convergence Behavior of Randomized Kaczmarz-type Methods for Solving Doubly Noisy Linear Systems
summary: The randomized Kaczmarz (RK) method is an efficient iterative projection algorithm with low computational complexity for solving consistent linear systems. However, noise is inevitable in real-world applications, and both the coefficient matrix and the right-hand side vector may be contaminated by noise. The convergence analysis of RK-type methods for doubly noisy linear systems, where both the system matrix and the measurement vector are perturbed, remains relatively limited. In this paper, we investigate the limiting behavior of the RK algorithm for solving doubly noisy inconsistent linear systems without imposing any additional initial assumptions. Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first convergence analysis of the randomized extended Kaczmarz (REK), randomized block Kaczmarz (RBK), and randomized double block Kaczmarz (RDBK) algorithms for doubly noisy linear systems. We prove that these algorithms converge to a neighborhood of the least-squares solution of the underlying noiseless system. Compared with existing theoretical estimates, the proposed bounds effectively characterize the convergence behavior of these algorithms when applied to doubly noisy linear systems. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical results.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the convergence behavior of various Kaczmarz-type algorithms (RK, REK, RBK, RDBK) when solving doubly noisy linear systems where both the coefficient matrix and right-hand side vector are perturbed. The authors prove these algorithms converge to a neighborhood of the least-squares solution of the underlying noiseless system, providing the first convergence analysis for REK, RBK, and RDBK in this doubly noisy setting.
AI.motivation: Real-world linear systems are inevitably contaminated by noise in both the coefficient matrix and the measurement vector, yet convergence analysis of Kaczmarz-type methods for doubly noisy systems remains limited. Existing work has not addressed the convergence behavior of extended and block variants of the Kaczmarz algorithm under such perturbations.
AI.method: The authors investigate the limiting behavior of the randomized Kaczmarz (RK) algorithm for doubly noisy inconsistent linear systems without imposing additional initial assumptions. They extend the convergence analysis to randomized extended Kaczmarz (REK), randomized block Kaczmarz (RBK), and randomized double block Kaczmarz (RDBK), proving convergence to a neighborhood of the least-squares solution of the noiseless underlying system.
AI.result: The paper provides the first convergence analysis for REK, RBK, and RDBK algorithms in the doubly noisy setting. The proposed error bounds effectively characterize convergence behavior and improve upon existing theoretical estimates. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: All four Kaczmarz-type algorithms converge to a neighborhood of the least-squares solution of the underlying noiseless system under doubly noisy conditions, with the derived bounds offering better characterization than prior work. The theoretical results are validated through numerical experiments.

title: Read, Write, Relax: Why Neural PDE Surrogates Need Both Global and Local Processing
summary: Recent mesh-based simulation advances have, in no small part, relied on neural surrogates of two distinct families: global models that route information through a small set of latent tokens, and local models that perform message passing across mesh edges. Consistent with both classes is the inability to perform beyond low-dimensional problems and small-scale or oversimplified meshes, the simulation regimes where industrial problems reside. Our work shows this explicitly and presents a unified formulation. In global approaches, latent-token attention acts as a spatial low-pass filter, while local message passing lacks the global reach necessary to propagate information across large mesh spaces. Viewed through the error, the two operators are the halves of a multigrid cycle: one corrects errors at the lower end of the spectrum, the other at the higher end, and neither can do the other's job. We introduce Read-Write-Relax (RWR), which interleaves latent attention with message-passing relaxation under a unified formulation. The interleaved processor lowers error across the entire spectrum, making RWR the most accurate model in nearly every comparison across our industrial and public benchmarks. It is also markedly data-efficient in the scarce-data regimes, accurate on the engineering quantities of interest, and scales full-field predictions to challenging, large-scale problems.

AI.tldr: RWR interleaves latent attention (global) with message-passing (local) in a unified formulation to address the spectral limitations of existing neural mesh surrogates, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, data efficiency, and scalability on industrial benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural surrogate models for mesh-based simulation—both global (latent-token attention) and local (message-passing) families—fail on industrial-scale problems characterized by high dimensionality and large/irregular meshes. Each family addresses only one half of the error spectrum (low or high frequency), and neither can handle the other's regime.
AI.method: The authors frame latent-token attention as a spatial low-pass filter and message passing as lacking global reach. They introduce Read-Write-Relax (RWR), a unified formulation that interleaves latent attention with message-passing relaxation steps, effectively combining both operators as complementary halves of a multigrid cycle to correct errors across the full spectrum.
AI.result: RWR achieves the highest accuracy in nearly every comparison across industrial and public benchmarks, demonstrates markedly better data efficiency in scarce-data regimes, maintains accuracy on engineering quantities of interest, and scales full-field predictions to challenging large-scale problems.
AI.conclusion: Unified interleaving of global and local operations is essential for industrial-grade mesh simulation, and RWR provides a principled, spectral-grounded framework that outperforms prior approaches across accuracy, data efficiency, and scalability.

title: Threshold dynamics of a time-periodic nonlocal dispersal SIS epidemic model with saturated incidence function and Neumann boundary conditions
summary: In this paper, we consider a time-periodic nonlocal dispersal susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) epidemic model with saturated incidence and Neumann boundary conditions in a spatiotemporally heterogeneous environment. First, we define the basic reproduction number for the model, which depends on dispersal rates, total population size and saturation parameters, and is quite different from those of models incorporating standard or bilinear incidence. Then, we establish its variational characterization and investigate the impacts of those parameters on it. Next, we explore the existence, uniqueness and global attractivity of the equilibria. We also analyze the asymptotic behaviors of endemic steady states for small saturation parameters, and for both small and large diffusion rates. Our results show that the saturation effect enables the total population size to have a significant impact on the disease dynamics. Furthermore, as the saturation parameter tends to zero, the basic reproduction number and the endemic equilibrium reduce to those of the standard-incidence model, respectively. Finally, we support our findings by numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a time-periodic nonlocal dispersal SIS epidemic model with saturated incidence and Neumann boundary conditions in a spatiotemporally heterogeneous environment, deriving the basic reproduction number, variational characterization, parameter impacts, equilibrium analysis, and asymptotic behaviors under various limits.
AI.motivation: To understand how saturation effects and nonlocal dispersal influence disease dynamics in heterogeneous environments, particularly how the total population size impacts the basic reproduction number in ways not seen in standard or bilinear incidence models.
AI.method: The authors define a basic reproduction number for the time-periodic nonlocal dispersal SIS model with saturated incidence, establish its variational characterization, analyze parameter impacts, study existence/uniqueness/global attractivity of equilibria, and examine asymptotic behaviors for small saturation parameters and both small and large diffusion rates, supplemented by numerical simulations.
AI.result: The saturation effect makes the total population size significantly influence disease dynamics, which differs from standard/bilinear incidence models. As the saturation parameter approaches zero, the basic reproduction number and endemic equilibrium converge to those of the standard-incidence model.
AI.conclusion: The saturation parameter fundamentally changes the mathematical structure and biological implications of the model, creating a novel dependence on total population size while maintaining a smooth connection to standard-incidence models as the saturation parameter tends to zero.

title: AI Surrogate Modeling for Real-Time Tokamak Equilibrium Prediction: Benchmarking Neural Architectures and Validation on EXL-50U
summary: Fast and reliable plasma equilibrium prediction is essential for real-time tokamak operation and control, but conventional Grad-Shafranov (GS) solvers are often too costly for real-time deployment. We develop an AI surrogate framework and benchmark five architectures (MLP, CNN, FNO, Transformer, and KAN) on a numerical GS database with 100,000 IID and 10,000 OOD samples. Under a unified protocol, we evaluate accuracy, inference efficiency, model scaling, and robustness. We also establish device-level validation on the EXL-50U tokamak by linking numerical GS solutions, surrogate predictions, and the standard Shape Editor reference to assess simulation-to-device consistency. The surrogates achieve errors of $10^{-3}$-$10^{-2}$ relative to GS solutions, while the GS-to-device discrepancy remains at $10^{-3}$. Transformer gives the best IID accuracy, whereas CNN offers the best balance of accuracy, robustness, and speed, reaching 0.7 ms TensorRT latency. On unseen plasma geometries and parameter regimes, CNN and FNO show the strongest extrapolation stability, with 4%-5% relative $L_2$ error, while models with weaker inductive biases degrade more substantially. Scaling data and model capacity improves interpolation but not necessarily extrapolation, revealing a trade-off between capacity and OOD generalization. Overall, this work provides a systematic, device-consistent benchmark for AI-based GS prediction and practical guidance for selecting reliable surrogates for real-time plasma control and fusion applications.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks five AI surrogate architectures (MLP, CNN, FNO, Transformer, KAN) for fast plasma equilibrium prediction using a 100k-sample Grad-Shafranov database, with device-level validation on the EXL-50U tokamak. CNN offers the best accuracy-robustness-speed balance (0.7ms TensorRT), while CNN and FNO show the strongest out-of-distribution extrapolation stability.
AI.motivation: Conventional Grad-Shafranov solvers are too computationally expensive for real-time tokamak operation and control, necessitating fast and reliable alternatives. A systematic benchmark of AI surrogates with device-level validation is needed to guide architecture selection for practical fusion applications.
AI.method: Develops an AI surrogate framework benchmarking five architectures (MLP, CNN, FNO, Transformer, KAN) on a numerical GS database (100,000 IID and 10,000 OOD samples) under a unified protocol evaluating accuracy, inference efficiency, model scaling, and robustness. Includes device-level validation on EXL-50U by linking numerical GS solutions, surrogate predictions, and the Shape Editor reference.
AI.result: Surrogates achieve 10^-3 to 10^-2 errors relative to GS solutions with GS-to-device discrepancy at 10^-3. Transformer excels at IID accuracy; CNN is best overall (0.7ms TensorRT latency). CNN and FNO show the strongest extrapolation (4-5% relative L2 error), while increasing data/model capacity improves interpolation but not extrapolation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a systematic, device-consistent benchmark for AI-based GS prediction and offers practical guidance for selecting reliable surrogates for real-time plasma control, highlighting a capacity versus out-of-distribution generalization trade-off.

title: Natural superconvergence points and asymptotic expansions for spline finite elements in one dimension
summary: We study the natural superconvergence points and asymptotic expansions of one-dimensional spline finite element approximations. For a spline space of degree $k$ and any smoothness $0\leμ\le k-1$, we prove that the $s$-th derivative of the error exhibits enhanced convergence of order $O(h^{k+2-s})$ at points where $k-s$ is even, provided the mesh is symmetric within a region of size $Ch|\ln h|$ around the point. This condition is known to be optimal for the cases of low derivative order $s=0,1$; the present analysis shows that the same local condition is sufficient for all admissible $s$. Moreover, by expanding the error in Legendre polynomials, a closure theorem determines the leading-order Legendre coefficients (the asymptotic expansion of the error) by combining the Galerkin orthogonality with the superconvergence conditions. For $μ=k-1$ (B-splines) and $μ=k-2$, the Galerkin orthogonality conditions vanish and the coefficients are determined solely by the superconvergence conditions. The asymptotic expansion can be expressed through a simple antiderivative recurrence on Legendre polynomials. The resulting polynomial's zeros encode the complete set of superconvergence points for all derivative orders. Numerical experiments for selected $(k,μ)$ pairs confirm the theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes superconvergence points and asymptotic expansions for one-dimensional spline finite element approximations, proving enhanced convergence of order O(h^{k+2-s}) at specific points under local mesh symmetry conditions, and deriving asymptotic expansions via Legendre polynomial expansions and a closure theorem.
AI.motivation: To establish optimal superconvergence conditions for all derivative orders in spline finite element methods, extending prior results that only covered low derivative orders s=0,1, and to provide a complete characterization of superconvergence points through asymptotic expansions.
AI.method: The paper proves superconvergence results for degree k splines with smoothness 0≤μ≤k−1, showing the s-th derivative error converges at order O(h^{k+2-s}) at points where k−s is even, given local mesh symmetry. It uses Legendre polynomial expansions of the error, a closure theorem combining Galerkin orthogonality with superconvergence conditions, and an antiderivative recurrence on Legendre polynomials for special cases (μ=k−1 and μ=k−2).
AI.result: The local mesh symmetry condition within a region of size Ch|ln h| is shown to be sufficient for all admissible derivative orders s, not just s=0,1. For B-splines (μ=k−1) and μ=k−2, Galerkin orthogonality conditions vanish and coefficients are determined solely by superconvergence conditions. The asymptotic expansion is expressible via a simple antiderivative recurrence, and the zeros of the resulting polynomial encode all superconvergence points for all derivative orders. Numerical experiments confirm the theory.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete theoretical framework for superconvergence in spline finite element methods across all derivative orders, with the condition identified as optimal for low derivative orders, and validates the approach through numerical experiments.

title: Regularized Subjective-Surface Flow with Monotone Reaction: Global Classical Well-Posedness and Stability
summary:
Touching and dividing cell nuclei may appear as connected structures in microscopy images, making it difficult to distinguish neighboring nuclei during segmentation. We introduce and analyze a regularized subjective-surface model designed for this setting. On a smooth bounded domain $Ω\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, the model is \[ u_t =
νΔu +
\left(\varepsilon^2+|\nabla u|^2\right)^{1/2} \operatorname{div}\!\left( G(x)\frac{\nabla u} {\left(\varepsilon^2+|\nabla u|^2\right)^{1/2}} \right) -
μΛ(x)H_η(u-q). \] Here, $\varepsilon>0$ and $ν>0$ are fixed regularization parameters, $G$ is a strictly positive smooth edge coefficient, and the nonnegative interaction weight $Λ$ incorporates fixed information about neighboring nucleus candidates. The principal objective of this work is to establish an existence theory for the proposed model. For compatible $C^{2+α}$ initial data taking values in $[0,1]$, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a global classical solution whose restriction to every finite time interval is Schauder-classical, together with preservation of the physical range, finite-time Schauder estimates, and $L^\infty$-nonexpansive dependence on the initial data. The main analytical step is a global spatial-gradient bound, obtained by combining gradient estimates near $\partialΩ$ with interior gradient estimates. These results provide a mathematical foundation for applying the model to the analysis of touching and dividing nuclei in 3D and 3D+time microscopy image data.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces and analyzes a regularized subjective-surface model (a modified Allen-Cahn type PDE) for segmenting touching and dividing cell nuclei in microscopy images. The authors prove existence and uniqueness of global classical solutions with compatible C^{2+α} initial data, establish physical range preservation, finite-time Schauder estimates, and L∞-nonexpansive dependence on initial data, via a key global spatial-gradient bound.
AI.motivation: Touching and dividing cell nuclei often appear as connected structures in microscopy images, making accurate segmentation difficult. A mathematically rigorous model is needed to distinguish neighboring nuclei, motivating the development and analysis of a regularized subjective-surface PDE that incorporates interaction weights from neighboring nucleus candidates.
AI.method: The authors propose a PDE model combining diffusion (νΔu), a regularized mean-curvature type term with edge coefficient G(x), and a reaction term with interaction weight Λ(x) and a smoothed Heaviside function H_η. The analytical framework uses Schauder theory, proving existence and uniqueness of global classical solutions via a global spatial-gradient bound obtained by combining boundary gradient estimates (near ∂Ω) with interior gradient estimates.
AI.result: The paper proves existence and uniqueness of a global classical solution for C^{2+α} initial data in [0,1], with preservation of the physical range, finite-time Schauder estimates, and L∞-nonexpansive dependence on initial data. The key technical achievement is a global spatial-gradient bound.
AI.conclusion: The established existence theory provides a solid mathematical foundation for applying the model to segment touching and dividing nuclei in 3D and 3D+time microscopy image data.

title: Helical jets driven by a ring of laser irradiation
summary: Plasma jets are formed in various astrophysical systems as plasma is rapidly ejected from a source, with a subset of these jets being magnetized and having a helical structure. Here, we demonstrate that helical jets may be formed using a ring of laser pulses that arrive on planar foils sequentially with increasing energy. The formation of the jets and their properties, including kinetic helicity, are studied through a set of three-dimensional magneto-hydrodynamics simulations with conditions informed by the parameters of the OMEGA laser facility. We find that jets with a higher degree of helicity may be generated under realistic experimental conditions when compared to a uniform jet. Synthetic x-ray and Thomson scattering diagnostics computed from simulated data demonstrate that the helical jet provides a unique fingerprint in both its morphology and plasma parameters. This laboratory helical jet platform may allow for controlled experimental study of the dynamics of helical plasma structures and, through interaction with other jets or targets, can allow for studies of shear-driven turbulence and mixing relevant to interactions between astrophysical jets and ambient clouds or crosswind.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that helical magnetized plasma jets, analogous to those found in astrophysical systems, can be formed in the laboratory using a ring of laser pulses that arrive on planar foils sequentially with increasing energy. Through 3D MHD simulations informed by OMEGA laser facility parameters, the authors show that these helical jets exhibit a higher degree of helicity than uniform jets and produce unique diagnostic fingerprints in x-ray and Thomson scattering measurements, enabling controlled experimental studies of helical plasma dynamics and jet interactions.
AI.motivation: Astrophysical plasma jets are often magnetized and helical in structure, but replicating these features in laboratory experiments has been challenging. Creating a controllable laboratory platform for helical jets would enable systematic studies of their dynamics and interactions.
AI.method: The authors use three-dimensional magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD) simulations with parameters informed by the OMEGA laser facility. They model a ring of laser pulses arriving on planar foils sequentially with increasing energy to generate helical jets, and compute synthetic x-ray and Thomson scattering diagnostics from the simulated data.
AI.result: The simulations show that helical jets with a higher degree of helicity can be generated under realistic experimental conditions compared to uniform jets. The synthetic diagnostics reveal a unique fingerprint of the helical jet in both its morphology and plasma parameters.
AI.conclusion: This laboratory helical jet platform may enable controlled experimental studies of helical plasma structure dynamics, and interactions with other jets or targets could facilitate research on shear-driven turbulence and mixing relevant to astrophysical jet interactions with ambient media.

title: Sharp CFL stability and temporal-dispersion optimization of symmetric splitting schemes for time-domain Maxwell equations
summary: We analyze coefficient design in a one-parameter family of explicit palindromic electric--magnetic splittings for the time-domain Maxwell equations. After fourth-order staggered spatial discretization, the Fourier amplification matrix depends on the single scalar $g_2=a(1-2a)/2$. We prove that $a=1/4$ is the unique real coefficient maximizing the spectral CFL interval, with threshold $s_*=12/(7\sqrt d)$. We then identify a real-coefficient obstruction to higher phase accuracy: cancellation of the leading temporal phase defect requires $g_2=1/12$, whereas every real member satisfies $g_2\le 1/16$. The resulting complex-conjugate coefficients give fourth-order temporal phase accuracy for each fixed semidiscrete Fourier mode and have threshold $6\sqrt3/(7\sqrt d)$, while the complete field update remains globally second order in time. For real Maxwell data, the physical output is the real projection of the complex trajectory; this projection is branch independent and preserves the second-order error bound. We further give an exactly equivalent doubled real-arithmetic realization, which clarifies the role of the auxiliary imaginary component without changing the numerical method. A semidiscrete convergence result and numerical experiments confirm the distinction between stability optimization and phase optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes coefficient design in a one-parameter family of explicit palindromic electric-magnetic splittings for time-domain Maxwell equations, proving that a=1/4 uniquely maximizes spectral stability (CFL threshold 12/(7√d)) while showing this choice is suboptimal for phase accuracy. The authors identify that achieving fourth-order temporal phase accuracy requires complex-conjugate coefficients (g2=1/12), which are shown to be unreachable by real coefficients (max g2≤1/16), and provide a doubled real-arithmetic realization with preserved second-order error bounds.
AI.motivation: To systematically analyze the trade-off between stability optimization and phase accuracy in explicit palindromic electric-magnetic splittings for time-domain Maxwell equations, and to resolve whether a single real coefficient can simultaneously maximize both spectral stability (CFL interval) and temporal phase accuracy.
AI.method: The authors derive the Fourier amplification matrix depending on a single scalar g2=a(1-2a)/2 after fourth-order staggered spatial discretization. They prove optimality of a=1/4 for spectral CFL via analytical arguments, demonstrate a real-coefficient obstruction (real g2 ≤ 1/16 vs. required g2=1/12 for phase accuracy), and introduce complex-conjugate coefficients with fourth-order phase accuracy per Fourier mode. They provide a branch-independent real projection for real Maxwell data and an exactly equivalent doubled real-arithmetic realization. A semidiscrete convergence result supports the analysis.
AI.result:
- a=1/4 uniquely maximizes spectral CFL interval with threshold s*=12/(7√d)
- Real coefficients cannot achieve g2=1/12 (required for leading temporal phase defect cancellation); max is 1/16
- Complex-conjugate coefficients achieve fourth-order temporal phase accuracy per Fourier mode with threshold 6√3/(7√d)
- The complete field update remains globally second order in time; real projection is branch independent and preserves second-order error
- An exactly equivalent doubled real-arithmetic realization is provided
- Numerical experiments confirm the stability vs. phase optimization distinction
AI.conclusion: Stability optimization (a=1/4) and phase optimization (complex coefficients with g2=1/12) are fundamentally incompatible within the real-coefficient family. Complex-conjugate coefficients provide superior phase accuracy at a modest CFL cost, while the real projection remains meaningful for physical data. This clarifies the design space and provides a practical doubled-real-arithmetic implementation path.

title: Pitch-controlled reorientational nonlinearity in chiral nematic liquid crystals: a reduced-order model for self-focusing and soliton formation
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures; published in Physical Review A 113, 033511 (2026)
summary: We present a reduced-order semi-analytical model for reorientational nonlinearity in chiral nematic liquid crystals, showing that the chiral pitch acts as the dominant physical length scale governing the onset of nonlinear self-focusing and soliton formation. Starting from the full Frank-Oseen equation, we derive a closed-form expression for the optically induced molecular rotation that captures the essential saturable response of the medium while reducing computational cost by more than two orders of magnitude compared with standard relaxation-method solvers. Despite its simplicity, the model reproduces the essential features of the numerically obtained nonlinear refractive index, the onset of self-localization, and the transition from discrete to continuous solitons in one and two dimensions. It further predicts the formation of fully localized astigmatic nematicons with only minor shifts in the self-localization threshold due to the neglect of nonlocal effects. The proposed model provides direct physical insight into light-matter interactions with soft matter media and offers a computationally efficient tool for the design and optimization of nonlinear photonic devices.

AI.tldr: A reduced-order semi-analytical model for reorientational nonlinearity in chiral nematic liquid crystals is presented, demonstrating that chiral pitch governs nonlinear self-focusing and soliton formation while reducing computational cost by over two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: To provide direct physical insight into light-matter interactions in chiral nematic liquid crystals while offering a computationally efficient alternative to standard relaxation-method solvers for modeling nonlinear self-focusing and soliton formation.
AI.method: Starting from the full Frank-Oseen equation, the authors derive a closed-form expression for optically induced molecular rotation that captures the saturable response of the medium, resulting in a reduced-order semi-analytical model.
AI.result: The model reproduces key numerical features including nonlinear refractive index behavior, onset of self-localization, and transition from discrete to continuous solitons in 1D and 2D. It predicts fully localized astigmatic nematicons with minor threshold shifts from neglected nonlocal effects, while reducing computational cost by more than two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The model offers a computationally efficient and physically insightful tool for designing and optimizing nonlinear photonic devices based on chiral nematic liquid crystals.

title: Shifted Horadam Collocation Method for Solution of Nonlinear Fourth-Order Boundary Value Problem in Ordinary Differential Equation
summary: In this paper, numerical solutions of a class of nonlinear ordinary differential equations are obtained using a collocation method based on the shifted Horadam polynomials. The proposed problem, which is of the fourth-order, satisfies a class of two-point boundary conditions. We first discuss definitions and basic properties of the Horadam polynomials before presenting new and useful differentiation formulae for them. Novel interesting identities are deduced from the differentiation properties. The collocation method under consideration assumes that the solution of the proposed problem can be expressed as a shifted Horadam polynomial series. To determine the expansion coefficients of the series solution, one collocates at the zeros of the shifted Horadam polynomials, and the proposed boundary value problem is subsequently reduced to a set of nonlinear algebraic equations. These algebraic equations are then solved using Newton's iterative method to obtain the numerical values of the expansion coefficients of the shifted Horadam polynomial series solution. Several examples of the proposed nonlinear boundary value problem are considered to demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, and reliability of the proposed method. Numerical solutions and errors obtained are compared with existing solutions. Comparisons of results, which are shown in tables and graphs, clearly reveal that the shifted Horadam collocation method outperforms the existing methods.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a collocation method using shifted Horadam polynomials to numerically solve fourth-order nonlinear ordinary differential equations with two-point boundary conditions. The method expands the solution as a shifted Horadam polynomial series, collocates at polynomial zeros to reduce the problem to nonlinear algebraic equations, and solves them via Newton's method. Numerical examples demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in accuracy and efficiency.
AI.motivation: To provide an accurate, efficient, and reliable numerical method for solving a class of fourth-order nonlinear ordinary differential equations with two-point boundary conditions, which are challenging to solve analytically.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) discussing definitions and basic properties of Horadam polynomials and presenting new differentiation formulae; (2) expressing the solution as a shifted Horadam polynomial series; (3) collocating at the zeros of shifted Horadam polynomials to reduce the boundary value problem to nonlinear algebraic equations; (4) solving these equations using Newton's iterative method to obtain expansion coefficients.
AI.result: Several numerical examples of the nonlinear boundary value problem were solved, comparing errors and solutions with existing methods. Results in tables and graphs show the shifted Horadam collocation method achieves superior accuracy, efficiency, and reliability compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The shifted Horadam collocation method is demonstrated to be an effective numerical approach that outperforms existing methods for solving fourth-order nonlinear boundary value problems.

title: A New Generalized Low-Rank Cholesky Factor ADI Algorithm for Large-Scale Stein Equations
summary:
The low-rank alternating direction implicit (ADI) method is an efficient solver for large-scale Stein equations with low-rank solutions. This paper shows that, as in the continuous-time Lyapunov equation case, the low-rank Cholesky factor ADI (LRCF-ADI) method for Stein equations implicitly performs $\mathcal{H}_2$-pseudo-optimal model order reduction for discrete-time systems. This observation leads to an automatic shift-generation strategy, allowing LRCF-ADI to select subsequent shifts without user intervention.
  The standard LRCF-ADI method requires shifts outside the unit circle. We generalize the method to allow shifts anywhere in the complex plane, including on the unit circle. This extension enables numerical integration for frequency-limited Stein equations by interpolating the integrand at points on the unit circle. It also enables non-intrusive, data-driven balanced truncation and frequency-limited balanced truncation using experimentally measurable transfer function samples on the unit circle, without requiring access to a state-space realization. Numerical results for large-scale models demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods as low-rank Stein equation solvers and data-driven model order reduction methods.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the low-rank Cholesky factor ADI (LRCF-ADI) method for Stein equations by showing it implicitly performs H2-pseudo-optimal model order reduction, enabling automatic shift selection. The method is generalized to allow shifts anywhere in the complex plane, enabling frequency-limited Stein equations and non-intrusive, data-driven balanced truncation from transfer function samples on the unit circle.
AI.motivation: The LRCF-ADI method for Stein equations requires user-specified shifts outside the unit circle, which limits its practical applicability and prevents broader use cases such as frequency-limited problems and data-driven model order reduction.
AI.method: The authors show that LRCF-ADI for Stein equations implicitly performs H2-pseudo-optimal model order reduction (analogous to the Lyapunov case), leading to an automatic shift generation strategy. They then generalize the method to permit shifts anywhere in the complex plane (including on the unit circle), which enables numerical integration for frequency-limited Stein equations and data-driven balanced truncation using transfer function samples on the unit circle without requiring a state-space realization.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on large-scale models demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods both as low-rank Stein equation solvers and as data-driven model order reduction techniques.
AI.conclusion: The generalized LRCF-ADI method with automatic shift selection and arbitrary complex-plane shifts provides a versatile framework for solving Stein equations and performing non-intrusive, data-driven model order reduction from transfer function measurements.

title: Cross-Temperature Defect Identification in Atomistic Simulations via Multi-Level Domain Alignment
summary: Identifying atomic defects at elevated temperature is difficult because thermal fluctuations blur the local symmetry that both geometric heuristics and supervised classifiers rely on: trustworthy labels exist in low-temperature reference configurations, while the high-temperature regime where robust analysis matters most is effectively unlabeled. We cast this as a cross-temperature domain-shift problem and align the two domains at three levels: an equivariant denoiser at the input level, cross-temperature contrastive learning at the representation level, and a morphology-aware regularizer that steers predictions toward the compact geometry of physical defect structures. Because no atom-wise truth exists at temperature, we further introduce a label-free evaluation suite that scores predicted defect structures along five spatial and physics-based axes, enabling model assessment and selection without high-temperature labels. Near the melting point, the framework identifies vacancies and self-interstitial atoms across face-centered-cubic, body-centered-cubic, and hexagonal-close-packed iron systems with every interstitial localized and zero false detections in every vacancy system against Wigner-Seitz ground truth, with no high-temperature labels used in training. It sustains this fidelity on a million-atom, 2.5 ns trajectory, resolving single vacancy hops and complete Frenkel-pair recombination, and captures grain-boundary phase transformations in aluminum bicrystals, distinguishing two nucleation modes. Multi-level domain alignment thus offers a practical, label-efficient route to temperature-robust structural analysis of large-scale molecular dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the challenge of identifying atomic defects at high temperatures by framing it as a cross-temperature domain-shift problem. The authors propose a multi-level alignment framework using an equivariant denoiser, cross-temperature contrastive learning, and a morphology-aware regularizer, plus a label-free evaluation suite. The method achieves perfect defect detection in iron systems near melting, scales to million-atom trajectories, and captures grain-boundary phase transformations.
AI.motivation: Atomic defect identification at elevated temperatures is difficult because thermal fluctuations blur local symmetry that both geometric heuristics and supervised classifiers rely on. Labels exist only in low-temperature reference configurations, while the high-temperature regime where robust analysis matters most is effectively unlabeled, creating a domain-shift problem.
AI.method: The framework aligns low- and high-temperature domains at three levels: (1) an equivariant denoiser at the input level, (2) cross-temperature contrastive learning at the representation level, and (3) a morphology-aware regularizer steering predictions toward compact physical defect geometry. Additionally, a label-free evaluation suite scores predicted defect structures along five spatial and physics-based axes for model assessment without high-temperature labels.
AI.result: Near the melting point, the framework identifies vacancies and self-interstitial atoms across FCC, BCC, and HCP iron systems with every interstitial localized and zero false detections in vacancy systems against Wigner-Seitz ground truth, using no high-temperature labels. It sustains fidelity on a million-atom, 2.5 ns trajectory, resolving single vacancy hops and complete Frenkel-pair recombination, and captures grain-boundary phase transformations in aluminum bicrystals with two nucleation modes distinguished.
AI.conclusion: Multi-level domain alignment offers a practical, label-efficient route to temperature-robust structural analysis of large-scale molecular dynamics simulations.

title: Uniform $L^2$ Non-Localization on Integrable Polygons: Eigenfunctions, Quasimodes, and Spectral Clusters

AI.tldr: This paper proves uniform L² non-localization for Dirichlet Laplacian eigenfunctions on all integrable polygonal domains (rectangles, isosceles right triangles, equilateral triangles, hemi-equilateral triangles), showing every positive-measure subset captures a uniformly positive fraction of mass for all eigenfunctions. The proof uses Schrödinger observability estimates on rectangular tori and equilateral triangles with reflection/symmetry reductions, and extends to Dirichlet Schrödinger operators with bounded potentials and to approximate eigenfunctions via defect estimates.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the polygonal localization problem—whether eigenfunctions can concentrate on small sets—completing the L² localization problem for the integrable subclass of polygons. This settles a fundamental question about quantum ergodicity/unique continuation properties on piecewise-linear domains.
AI.method: The proof leverages known Schrödinger observability estimates on rectangular tori and equilateral triangles, combined with reflection and symmetry reductions to transfer these estimates to the polygonal domains with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Since Schrödinger evolution acts by a scalar phase on each eigenspace, the stationary estimate becomes uniform over the entire eigenspace, handling spectral multiplicity.
AI.result: The paper establishes uniform L² non-localization for the complete class of integrable polygons. It extends results to Dirichlet Schrödinger operators with real-valued bounded potentials on rectangles and isosceles right triangles, and provides explicit defect estimates for approximate eigenfunctions, ensuring uniform lower mass bounds for quasimodes and spectral clusters.
AI.conclusion: The integrable subclass of the polygonal localization problem is now completely resolved with a uniform non-localization result, valid even with spectral multiplicity, and with extensions to bounded potentials and approximate eigenfunctions.

title: On the extreme eigenvalues of the Gram Matrix in Physics-Informed Neural Networks for the Poisson Equation
summary: The smallest and largest eigenvalues of the Gram matrix induced by the differential neural tangent kernel (DNTK) play a pivotal role in the analysis of over-parameterized PINNs trained by gradient type algorithms. However, a theoretical analysis of the extreme eigenvalues remains completely absent due to the challenge posed by the presence of multiple differential operators. In this work, we provide explicit lower and upper bounds for the extreme eigenvalues of the infinite DNTK matrix for the Poisson equation with the Dirichlet boundary condition for two-layer RePU neural networks without the bias term. The setting is fairly general with respect to the sampling points and input dimension \(d\): \(δ\)-separated and additionally \(d\geq 3\) when deriving the lower bound of the smallest eigenvalue. These results extend that for the neural tangent kernel, and to the best of our knowledge, represent the first results on the spectrum of the DNTK.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first theoretical bounds (lower and upper) for the extreme eigenvalues of the infinite differential neural tangent kernel (DNTK) matrix for the Poisson equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions, using two-layer RePU neural networks without bias, extending prior results from the standard NTK setting.
AI.motivation: The extreme eigenvalues of the DNTK-induced Gram matrix are crucial for analyzing over-parameterized physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) trained with gradient-type algorithms. However, no theoretical results exist for these eigenvalues due to the complexity introduced by multiple differential operators in the DNTK.
AI.method: The authors derive explicit lower and upper bounds for the extreme eigenvalues of the infinite DNTK matrix for the Poisson equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions, considering two-layer RePU neural networks without bias. The analysis applies to δ-separated sampling points, and additionally requires d≥3 for the lower bound of the smallest eigenvalue.
AI.result: Explicit bounds on the smallest and largest eigenvalues of the infinite DNTK matrix are established, extending existing results from the neural tangent kernel to the differential setting. These are stated to be the first results on the DNTK spectrum.
AI.conclusion: This work fills a fundamental gap in the theoretical analysis of PINNs by providing rigorous spectral bounds for the DNTK, which are essential for convergence and generalization guarantees of gradient-based training in over-parameterized PINNs.

title: DAW: Dynamics-Aware Weighting for Deep Learning Forecasts of Chaotic Systems
summary: Deep learning surrogates for forecasting chaotic dynamical systems suffer from catastrophic error accumulation over long-term autoregressive rollouts. This behavior is partly tied to the underlying systems: chaotic spatiotemporal systems, such as the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation, visit phase space unevenly - dominated by recurrent, low-dimensional quiescent states (e.g., near-laminar flows) and punctuated by rare, dynamically complex topological transitions (e.g., wave-merging events). Under a sample-wise uniform objective, standard neural surrogates allocate their finite capacity to the statistically numerous quiescent states, under-representing the transient regimes that trigger disproportionate, localized errors. Existing imbalanced-regression methods reweight samples by target-space density. However, statistical target-space rarity need not coincide with the intrinsic dynamical rarity - the recurrence geometry of the attractor that is the source of the imbalance. To address this, we introduce Dynamics-Aware Weighting (DAW), a data-centric objective reweighting framework. Using the local dimension $d$ from dynamical systems theory as an a priori measure of a state's active degrees of freedom, DAW reshapes the loss landscape to allocate representational capacity toward the sparse, high-$d$ regimes where forecast errors are systematically large.
